description: Fingerprints, DNA, specialist squads, community policing and the digital age of law enforcement.
content_html:
Policing in the Twentieth Century

The police forces created in the nineteenth century faced radically new challenges as the twentieth century progressed. Faster criminals, more complex crimes and growing cities all demanded new tools and new ways of working. The response took three main forms: new technologies, specialist units, and — particularly from the 1980s onwards — community-based approaches designed to rebuild trust between police and public.

Transport and Communications

The motor car transformed policing before it transformed crime. From the 1900s, forces began acquiring vehicles to pursue faster criminals and respond to incidents across larger areas. By the interwar period, police forces had radio-equipped cars, and the “999” emergency telephone system was introduced in London in 1937 — a service that seemed revolutionary at the time and created the expectation of rapid police response that the public has held ever since. Control rooms evolved from simple telephone exchanges into sophisticated computer-aided dispatch centres by the 1980s and 1990s.

Key Fact

The 999 emergency system was introduced in London in 1937. It transformed public expectations of policing, creating the assumption of rapid response, and required forces to invest heavily in radio communications, vehicles and control room infrastructure.

Fingerprinting and Scientific Evidence

The late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries saw the application of science to criminal detection for the first time. Fingerprinting was introduced to Scotland Yard in 1901, following the pioneering work of Francis Galton and Edward Henry. The technique allowed detectives to link suspects to crime scenes with objective physical evidence, transforming the investigative process. The first English conviction based primarily on fingerprint evidence came in 1902.

The twentieth century saw further scientific advances. Forensic pathology, blood typing, ballistics analysis and the examination of trace evidence (hair, fibres, soil) all became standard parts of serious crime investigations. The most transformative development came in 1984, when Professor Sir Alec Jeffreys at the University of Leicester discovered DNA profiling. First used in a criminal investigation in 1986 to identify a murderer in Leicestershire, DNA evidence rapidly became the most powerful tool in forensic science. By the 1990s, the National DNA Database had been established, allowing detectives to link crime scene DNA to suspects on an unprecedented scale.

Key Fact

DNA profiling was developed by Professor Sir Alec Jeffreys at the University of Leicester in 1984 and first used in a criminal investigation in 1986. It has since become the most powerful tool in forensic science, enabling convictions (and exonerations) that previous investigative methods could never have achieved.

As crime became more complex, generalised policing became less adequate. Specialist units developed within police forces to tackle particular types of crime. Special Branch was established in 1883 to counter Irish republican terrorism — making it one of the first specialist security units in British policing. The Flying Squad, established in 1919, specialised in serious robberies and was notable for its use of vehicles and rapid response. The Serious Fraud Office was created in 1987 to tackle complex financial crime beyond the capacity of ordinary detective units. Counter-terrorism policing has expanded dramatically since 2001.

Community policing emerged as a formal strategy from the 1980s, partly in response to serious breakdowns in police-public relations — the Scarman Report (1981) following the Brixton riots highlighted how aggressive policing tactics had damaged trust in inner-city communities. The concept was that policing was most effective when officers knew their areas well, worked alongside local people, and addressed the underlying conditions that bred crime (unemployment, poor housing, drug dependency) rather than simply responding to incidents.

The Police Reform Act of 2002 created Police Community Support Officers (PCSOs) — uniformed civilians who could patrol communities, engage with residents and deal with minor anti-social behaviour without the full powers of a sworn officer. PCSOs were controversial: critics argued they were a cheap substitute for real officers; supporters pointed to their success in community engagement. By the 2010s, however, austerity cuts had reduced PCSO numbers significantly.

Neighbourhood Watch and Public Involvement

Technology alone could not solve the problem of community trust. From the early 1980s, Neighbourhood Watch schemes spread rapidly across Britain, following an American model first introduced in the 1970s. By the early 1990s, over five million households had joined a scheme, making it one of the largest voluntary crime prevention movements in British history. The scheme reflected a recognition that the police could not be everywhere: effective crime prevention depended on the eyes and knowledge of the communities themselves.

Neighbourhood Watch worked best in stable, owner-occupied suburban areas where residents knew each other. In high-turnover urban areas with transient populations, schemes were harder to establish and sustain. Critics noted that Neighbourhood Watch could entrench social exclusion — leading to suspicion of unfamiliar faces rather than genuine community safety. The scheme nonetheless demonstrated a broader shift in policing thinking: reducing crime was a shared responsibility between police and public, not simply a matter of more officers or better technology.

Policing the Digital Age

From the 1980s and accelerating through the 1990s and 2000s, CCTV became a defining feature of British public space. By the 2000s, Britain had more CCTV cameras per person than almost any other country in the world, with cameras covering high streets, transport hubs, stadiums and car parks. Footage from CCTV systems became a routine part of criminal investigations — the 2005 London bombings investigation relied heavily on camera footage to identify the attackers within days. Proponents argued CCTV both deterred crime and aided detection; civil liberties groups raised concerns about mass surveillance of innocent people in public spaces.

Computer databases transformed police record-keeping and intelligence sharing from the 1980s onwards. The Police National Computer (PNC), introduced in 1974, allowed forces across Britain to check vehicle and criminal records in seconds rather than hours. The combination of PNC access, DNA databases, CCTV footage and digital communications meant that by the early twenty-first century, modern policing operated within an intelligence infrastructure entirely unrecognisable to a 1950s beat officer.
exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark ‘Explain Change’ question on twentieth-century policing, focus on a specific technology (fingerprinting from 1901, DNA profiling from 1984) or a specific development (999 system 1937, specialist units, community policing). Examiners want you to explain how the change improved policing, not just name it. For a 16-mark thematic essay comparing policing across all eras, the shift from community responsibility (Saxon tithings) to professional forces (1829) to technological/specialised policing (twentieth century) is the key three-era framework — make sure you argue a judgement about which change was most significant.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 999 emergency system (1937) and police radio transformed the public’s expectation of rapid response; control rooms evolved into sophisticated computer-aided dispatch centres by the late twentieth century.
  • Fingerprinting (introduced 1901) and DNA profiling (developed 1984 by Alec Jeffreys; first used in a case 1986) represent the most significant technological advances in criminal investigation, enabling detectives to link suspects to crime scenes with objective physical evidence.
  • Community policing emerged in the 1980s as a response to damaged police-public relations; Neighbourhood Watch schemes from 1982 and PCSOs from 2002 extended the reach of policing into everyday community life.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of DNA profiling as a tool of criminal investigation.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. Feature may include: developed by Alec Jeffreys in 1984; first used in a criminal case in 1986; identifies individuals from their unique genetic code; led to the National DNA Database; can both convict and exonerate suspects. Simple identification (1 mark); developed with date or significance (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of developments in police communications in the twentieth century.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: The 999 emergency telephone system was introduced in London in 1937, transforming public expectations of rapid police response and requiring investment in radio communications and vehicles. Feature 2: Control rooms evolved from simple telephone exchanges into computer-aided dispatch centres by the 1980s-1990s, enabling the coordination of officers and vehicles across large force areas in real time.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why specialist police units became necessary in the twentieth century.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Names a specialist unit. Developing: Notes crime became more complex. Secure: Explains how increasingly sophisticated crime (organised robbery, terrorism, serious fraud) exceeded the capacity of generalist detective work; uses a specific example such as Special Branch (1883, terrorism), Flying Squad (1919, serious robberies) or the Serious Fraud Office (1987); explains why specialisation was the logical response to increasing criminal complexity. Mastering: Sustains analysis linking the nature of new crimes to the specific capabilities required, evaluates whether specialisation improved overall effectiveness or created fragmented policing.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the introduction of fingerprinting in 1901 for criminal investigation in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: States fingerprinting was introduced. Developing: Notes it allowed suspects to be linked to crime scenes. Secure: Analyses significance at the time: objective physical evidence transformed detective work; the first conviction based on fingerprint evidence came in 1902; it reduced reliance on witness testimony and confession alone. Mastering: Evaluates significance over time: fingerprinting established the principle of scientific evidence in court that was later extended by blood typing, ballistics and DNA; compares the investigative landscape before 1901 (reliance on witness testimony and informers) with after; judges fingerprinting as the beginning of the forensic revolution in policing.

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree that technology was the most important factor in improving policing in the twentieth century?
Give reasons for your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments for technology: fingerprinting (1901), DNA profiling (1984), 999 system (1937), computers and databases dramatically improved detection rates and response times. Against — other factors important: specialist units tackled crime types technology alone cannot address; community policing rebuilt trust where technology actually increased distance (patrol cars replaced foot patrols); organisational reforms (1856 inspection, accountability frameworks) set the foundation. Emerging: one-sided. Developing: notes other factors. Secure: argues a position, uses specific evidence from multiple developments. Mastering: weighs technology against other factors with sustained analysis, reaches a justified conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of community policing that developed from the 1980s onwards.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: Community policing emphasised building long-term relationships between officers and local communities, prioritising prevention and addressing underlying social causes of crime (unemployment, poor housing, drugs) rather than solely reactive enforcement. Feature 2: The Police Reform Act 2002 created Police Community Support Officers (PCSOs) — uniformed civilian staff who could patrol, engage with residents and deal with minor anti-social behaviour, extending the policing presence without the cost of sworn officers.

knowledge_checks.q: In what year was the 999 emergency telephone system introduced in London?
Fingerprinting was introduced to Scotland Yard in _____, following the work of Francis Galton and Edward Henry.
The _____ Report of 1981 highlighted how aggressive policing tactics had damaged trust in inner-city communities, contributing to the development of community policing strategies.
Match each specialist unit to its primary function:
right: Civilian uniformed staff for community engagement, created 2002

flashcard_questions.q: When was the 999 emergency system introduced in London?
What is fingerprinting and when was it introduced to Scotland Yard?
flashcard_questions.a: The identification of individuals by unique ridge patterns on fingertips — introduced in 1901.

flashcard_questions.q: Who developed DNA profiling and in what year?
flashcard_questions.a: Professor Sir Alec Jeffreys, University of Leicester, in 1984.

flashcard_questions.q: When was DNA profiling first used in a criminal investigation in England?
flashcard_questions.a: 1986, to identify a murderer in Leicestershire.

flashcard_questions.q: When was Special Branch established and for what original purpose?
What was the Flying Squad, and when was it established?
flashcard_questions.a: A Metropolitan Police unit specialising in serious robberies, established in 1919.
An approach emphasising long-term relationships with communities, prioritising prevention over reactive law enforcement.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Scarman Report (1981) reveal about policing in Britain?
flashcard_questions.a: Aggressive policing tactics had damaged trust in inner-city communities, contributing to the Brixton riots.

flashcard_questions.q: What are Police Community Support Officers (PCSOs)?
flashcard_questions.a: Uniformed civilian staff created by the Police Reform Act 2002 to support officers and engage with communities.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a police control room?
flashcard_questions.a: A headquarters receiving 999 calls and coordinating deployment of officers and vehicles across a force area.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one way DNA profiling has changed criminal justice beyond convictions.
flashcard_questions.a: It has also exonerated wrongly convicted individuals by proving their DNA did not match crime scene samples.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did community policing emerge as a formal strategy in the 1980s?
flashcard_questions.a: Following serious breakdowns in police-public relations, particularly after the Brixton riots (1981).

glossary_terms.definition: Police operational headquarters that receives 999 calls and coordinates the deployment of officers and vehicles across a force area.
The system of identifying individuals by the unique patterns of ridges on their fingertips, used in criminal investigation from 1901 onwards.
A forensic technique that identifies individuals from their unique genetic code, first used in a criminal investigation in England in 1986.
A unit of the Metropolitan Police, established in 1883, originally to counter Irish republican terrorism and later to cover all domestic and international counter-terrorism intelligence.
An approach to policing that emphasises building long-term relationships between officers and the communities they serve, prioritising prevention and partnership over reactive law enforcement.
Police Community Support Officers: uniformed civilian staff who support regular police officers, engaging with communities, conducting patrols and dealing with minor disorder.
